picks.excerpt: Library ebook-lending app Libby will let readers filter out AI-narrated and AI-written titles — but the filters rely on AI content being self-labeled by publishers, raising questions about how effective the screening can really be.
picks.rationale: A reader-facing AI filter in a major library app is concretely actionable and probes the self-labeling loophole — reputable outlet, fresh, never covered.

picks.excerpt: Michael Caine has licensed an AI-generated version of his voice to narrate an audiobook adaptation of Homer's Odyssey, produced with voice-AI company ElevenLabs — a marquee case of a major actor formally licensing, rather than fighting, an AI voice clone for a literary work.
picks.rationale: Marquee precedent: an A-list actor licensing (not fighting) an AI voice clone for an audiobook resets the voice-rights conversation for publishing.

picks.excerpt: More than 250 UK publishers have opted in to Publishers' Licensing Services' collective AI licensing scheme, which lets publishers jointly manage and monetize licensing of their content to AI companies — a concrete counter-model to unlicensed scraping.
picks.rationale: 250+ publishers signing a collective AI licensing scheme is a concrete industry counter-model to scraping; preferred over the same outlet's vaguer PLS-conference piece.

picks.excerpt: Fiction-writing tool Sudowrite added Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5 as a writing model in its June 30 update, alongside folder exports and keyboard-accessible document reordering — a fresh model upgrade for AI-assisted novelists.
picks.rationale: Most tool-actionable pick: a new frontier writing model landing in a dedicated fiction tool changes how AI-assisted authors work tomorrow.

picks.excerpt: US AI companies are reportedly buying large quantities of secondhand books in German-speaking markets — scanning then destroying them — to train language models, while an Australian survey finds 17.4% of audiobook listeners have already tried AI narration.
picks.rationale: Roundup allowed by exception: its lead — AI firms buying, scanning and destroying secondhand books for training data — is striking, fresh and covered nowhere else in the pool.
